Login succeeds, but a refresh signs the user out. Help me check whether the session cookie is set and sent back with requests.

A cookie is a small piece of data the browser stores by server rules and sends automatically on matching later requests.·For example, a login response uses Set-Cookie to store a session identifier. When the browser later visits a matching address, it sends a Cookie request header so the server can find the session. A cookie is only part of the request round trip, not a complete authentication system, authorization decision, or database; sensitive sessions also need properties such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite.

The cookie has not completed a round trip yetA cookie is not a database and does not replace server-side authorization.
The three steps in a cookie round trip

The response asks the browser to store it: The server sends Set-Cookie in a response, and the browser decides whether to store it from its name, scope, and security attributes.

Later requests send it when conditions match: For a matching address, the browser puts sendable cookies in the Cookie request header. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by page script but can still be sent with a request.

What it is not

Cookies and localStorage can both keep data in a browser, but cookies enter HTTP requests by rule. A cookie is not a complete authentication system or a database; the server must still verify the session, identity, and permission for each action. Sensitive sessions should use Secure and HttpOnly over HTTPS and choose SameSite for the cross-site need.
